turns.content: ok so i need your take on something real quick. like genuinely, if someone leaves a text on read for 4 days but is actively posting on ig stories in that time, is that basically just them choosing to avoid the conversation? not like they forgot or missed it, right?

Yeah, mostly. Four days plus active story posting means they've had their phone in hand and had the bandwidth to pick a filter, so "didn't see it" is off the table. They saw it.

But "choosing to avoid the conversation" covers a few different flavors, and they're not all equally bad:

- **Actively dodging you.** They don't want to have that specific conversation and are hoping it dies quietly. This is what it feels like, and sometimes it's exactly that.
- **The reply feels like work.** If your text needed a real answer (plans, feelings, a decision), some people open it, think "I'll do this properly later," and then later never comes. Stories are zero-effort; a thoughtful reply isn't. Not a great excuse, but it's a real pattern and it's not always personal.
- **Avoidant by default.** Some people are just like this with everyone and genuinely don't register that four days reads as a statement.

The thing is, from your side it kind of doesn't matter which one it is. Whatever the reason, they decided posting was worth their time and answering you wasn't, and you're allowed to take that information at face value. If you care about this person, one low-pressure follow-up ("hey, no rush, just checking you saw this") is fair. If they blow through that too, you have your answer, and it's not about you forgetting to say the right thing.

What did the text say, roughly? That changes which bucket I'd bet on.

ok so here's the full thing. this is about my old roommate julian. i sent him a text 4 days ago saying the $300 deposit for the cabin is due tonight at midnight. he left it on read. meanwhile he's been posting ig stories, like multiple a day, during finals week. so he's clearly seen it and just decided not to answer, right? like that's not stress, that's him dodging me on purpose. i need to cancel his spot by midnight or i lose the $300. thoughts?

Yeah, he's seen it. Multiple stories a day means he's on his phone plenty. But I'd push back a little on "that's not stress, that's dodging on purpose," because those two things aren't opposites. Finals-week story posting is *exactly* what stress-avoidance looks like: mindless, zero-commitment phone stuff feels fine, but a text that says "give me $300 by midnight" is a decision he doesn't want to make, so he keeps not making it. That's still avoidance, and it's still on him. It just probably isn't a personal statement about you.

And here's the part that actually matters: it doesn't change what you should do tonight. His reasons are his problem. Your problem is $300 with a deadline.

So, right now, before you spiral further:

1. **Send one blunt, unmissable text.** Not passive-aggressive, just clear: "Julian, cabin deposit is due at midnight. If I don't hear a yes + $300 from you by 9pm I'm cancelling your spot so I don't lose the money. No hard feelings either way." Give yourself a buffer before the actual midnight cutoff.
2. **Call him.** Once. It's a lot harder to leave a ringing phone on read, and it moves the burden fully onto him.
3. **If nothing by your cutoff, cancel his spot.** Don't cover it hoping he'll pay you back. You are not the one who should be eating $300 because someone couldn't type "yes" or "no" in four days.

If he pops up later all "wait, I still wanted to go," that's a fair conversation to have, but it's *his* mess to clean up, not yours. You gave him four days and a heads-up. That's more than enough.

ok so you're saying it could be stress and not personal. i get that. but here's the thing — you agreed ignoring texts while posting stories is avoidance. you said it's on him. and now the deadline is tonight and he's done nothing. so is it fair to say he intentionally chose not to pay? like that's the logical endpoint of 4 days of silence + stories + missing a deadline, right?

Close, but not quite, and the gap matters a little for how you talk to him after.

What the evidence supports: he saw the text, had the bandwidth to reply, and chose not to deal with it for four days. That's intentional avoidance. I'll stand by that.

What it doesn't quite prove: that he made a conscious decision "I'm not paying." Those are different things. Avoidance is usually *not deciding*, over and over, until the deadline decides for you. He may have never once thought "I'm out." He just kept thinking "ugh, later." Functionally, for your wallet, it's identical. Morally, it's a bit different, and it matters because it changes what he's going to say when he resurfaces. Someone who deliberately opted out will shrug. Someone who avoided will go "wait what, I didn't realize it was tonight," which will be maddening but will also be, in his head, true.

So the fair framing is: he didn't choose not to pay, he chose not to engage, and not engaging past a deadline has the same result as a no. You're allowed to treat it as a no. You don't have to prove intent to protect your $300.

Which is why I'd still send the one blunt text with a cutoff, then cancel. That text does two things: it gives him a last real chance, and it means when he pops up later, you've got receipts that you didn't just silently drop him. Then the "did you mean it or did you just dodge" conversation, if you even want it, happens on your terms and not with a $300 clock ticking.
